claims.text: The Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles are sub-10 nm and equiatomic, corresponding to approximately 20 at.% of each element.
The as-fabricated nanoparticles are initially a single-phase solid solution.
The initial equiatomic solid solution has high configurational entropy.
The proposed intervention heats the nanoparticles in vacuum from 300 K to 1000 K.
Using vacuum eliminates oxidation effects analogous to those seen in Mn-containing HEAs.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down for particles below approximately 5 nm and at temperatures above approximately 800 K.
Elevated-temperature HEAs can exhibit rapid, element-selective transport rather than universally sluggish behavior.
Au or Cu has sufficiently high diffusivity in these nanoparticles to mediate their structural evolution.
At sub-10 nm sizes, surface-energy contributions overwhelm stabilization from bulk configurational entropy.
Surface-energy minimization creates a thermodynamic driving force for rapid phase separation.
Low-surface-energy Au segregates to nanoparticle surfaces or produces core-shell structures.
A high surface chemical-potential gradient overcomes sluggish diffusion and causes rapid atomic exchange.
Ostwald ripening dissolves smaller particles and transfers their material to larger particles.
Heating produces Au-rich and Co/Cu/Ni/Pt-rich domains.
Heating significantly reduces the number density of particles below 5 nm through dissolution.
Particles change from spherical shapes to faceted or elongated shapes during heating.
Phase separation will cause lattice-parameter changes and XRD peak broadening or splitting.
Bulk high-entropy models predict that configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion preserve a single-phase solid solution up to 1000 K.
For particles larger than 20 nm, bulk thermodynamic stabilization and sluggish diffusion may prevail.
Below 600 K, diffusion is too slow for phase separation within an hours-long experiment.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis places the size breakdown threshold at about 5 nm, whereas the mechanism and boundary broadly apply surface-dominated behavior to all sub-10 nm particles without resolving the 5–10 nm regime.

The mechanism says shape evolution minimizes total surface area, but the predicted elongated morphology would generally have greater surface area than a sphere of equal volume unless anisotropic facet energies are explicitly invoked.
